newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac meets Arafat over peace deadlock.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac meets Arafat over peace deadlock.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac met Yasser Arafat on Monday and warned that deadlock in the Middle East peace process could trigger widespread guerrilla violence.

The French leader said the United States and Europe must do all they could to bring about a resumption in peace talks and convince Israel and the Palestinians to implement their Oslo accord on Palestinian autonomy.

"The French people are very worried about reactions to the deadlock which could cause uncontrolled terrorist actions that would destabilise the region as well as the United States and Europe," Chirac told reporters after discussing ways to end the Middle East impasse over lunch with Palestinian President Arafat.
Formal Israeli-Palestinian peace moves came to a halt in March after Israel broke ground for a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

A Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) official in Jerusalem who insisted on anonymity said before Arafat left for his day-long visit that he had been invited at short notice by Chirac "for important talks on the peace process".
He said Europeans had asked France to play a leading role in breaking the deadlock and co-ordinate with the United States to return to play a role in solving the crisis.

Arafat, president of the West Bank and Gaza areas transferred to Palestinian rule under a peace deal with Israel, was scheduled to hold his first talks later in the afternoon with France's new left-wing Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine.
An alliance of Socialists, Communists and Greens swept to power in France in a June 1 parliamentary election, forcing the conservative Chirac to share power with a leftist government.

He was also to sign a financial aid agreement to provide the autonomous Palestinian areas with 90 million francs ($16 million) in aid for 1997, an increase of five million francs ($900,000) over last year.
A foreign ministry spokesman said aid to the Palestinians was the sole French assistance programme to increase this year. The funds are intended for water and business projects.
Arafat and Chirac shook hands and embraced on the stairs of the Elysee presidential palace before starting their meeting.
Chirac has tried hard in the past to involve France in the negotiations, but Israel has resisted giving it a key role, seeing Paris as biased in favour of the Arab states.
Jospin has criticised France's previous rightist government, accusing it of paying too little attention to the views of Israel in formulating policy.

A role for Paris in the super-sensitive peace process would take on a new dynamic in view of Chirac's sharing of power with Jospin. The two men have vowed to speak with a single voice in managing French affairs, but after a month of power-sharing their first hints at differences have begun to emerge.
